analysis.one_liner: Sets enforceable standards for immigrant detention, phases out private detention, and ends mandatory detention of asylum seekers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: with 128 House Democrats cosponsoring, it sat in two House committees until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set binding minimum conditions for the roughly 30,000 immigrants held by Immigration and Customs Enforcement on any given day, with unannounced inspections, fines, and the right to sue over violations. It would have required the government to stop contracting with private prison companies and local jails within three years, banned detaining children and solitary confinement, and replaced automatic detention of asylum seekers with a hearing and a presumption of release. It also would have made detention contracts and inspection reports public.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants in detention and their families gain enforceable conditions of confinement, faster court hearings, a presumption of release, and the ability to sue when standards are violated [S3]. Taxpayers gain transparency into contracts and a shift toward community-based supervision, which costs a fraction of bed-based detention [S3]. People who fear being picked up by immigration agents gain a required probable-cause hearing within 48 hours and a ban on stops based on language or appearance [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires detention standards at least as protective as the American Bar Association's Civil Immigration Detention Standards, enforced through annual unannounced Inspector General inspections, fines of at least 10% of a facility's contract for first failures, and contract termination or shutdown for repeat failures [S2][S3].
Gives detained individuals the right to sue in federal court for injuries caused by violations of the standards, with injunctive relief, damages, and attorney fees available [S3].
Requires notice to Congress within 24 hours of any death in custody, an investigation with a root-cause analysis within 30 days, and a public report within 60 days [S2][S3].

Bans detaining anyone under 18 in ICE facilities, bans solitary confinement, abolishes mandatory detention for asylum seekers, and requires a custody hearing with a presumption of release and bond amounts based on ability to pay [S2][S3].

Phases out within three years all contracts with for-profit detention companies and the use of local jails, requiring that facilities be owned and operated by the government or, for alternatives to detention, by nonprofits [S2][S3].

Creates a community-based case management program outside ICE offering housing, medical care, legal services, and transportation, with no electronic ankle monitors and no fees charged to participants [S3].

Makes detention contracts and inspection reports subject to public records requests, requires a monthly public 'facilities matrix' with population and compliance data, and requires the online detainee locator to update within 12 hours [S3].

Prohibits immigration officers from interrogating people based on race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, sexual orientation, or spoken language, and requires a probable-cause hearing before a judge within 48 hours of a warrantless arrest [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private prison companies (such as GEO Group and CoreCivic), which hold most ICE detainees under federal contracts, lose their detention business over three years, as do county jails that rent beds to ICE [S3]. Taxpayers and DHS bear the cost of building, owning, and operating government-run facilities and nonprofit-run supervision programs to replace them [S3]. The immigration enforcement agencies also lose tools: automatic detention of asylum seekers, ankle monitors as a supervision option, and expedited warrantless arrests [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison companies, county jails, and DHS

drawbacks.text: Requiring the government to own and operate all detention facilities and alternatives-to-detention programs within three years is a costly restructuring; Congress would have to appropriate money to build or take over facilities now run by contractors [S3].

The bill creates a presumption of release that the government can rebut only with clear and convincing evidence, and bars relying on a criminal record as the sole reason to keep someone detained — critics of similar measures argue this makes it harder to hold people with serious records during removal proceedings, though the bill retains a public-safety exception and allows detention of people ordered removed who pose a risk [S3].

Banning ankle monitors and electronic surveillance as conditions of supervision removes the tracking tool the government currently uses for people released into the community, which could make some judges and agencies reluctant to release rather than detain [S3].

Releasing most asylum seekers and other detainees into community-based supervision instead of beds reduces detention capacity, which opponents of the bill's approach argue weakens enforcement of immigration court appearances even though case management programs historically show higher appearance rates than bond alone [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and far-reaching for a population held largely without enforceable standards: independent inspections, a right to sue, no child detention, no solitary, and an end to paying private companies per detained bed. The main honest cost is fiscal and administrative — standing up government-owned facilities and nonprofit case management within three years would be expensive and logistically difficult, and shifting the detention burden onto the government to prove necessity would change enforcement practice significantly. Weighing those against the human and financial cost of the current contract-based detention system, the trade favors the bill's approach; the three-year phase-out timeline was generous by the standards of similar proposals.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary and Homeland Security committees for the entire Congress — neither committee ever held a markup or brought it to the floor — and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on March 26, 2021, joined as an original cosponsor by Rep. Adam Smith of Washington [S1][S3].

It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Homeland Security Committee, and then to the Border Security subcommittee the next day and the Immigration and Citizenship subcommittee in October 2021 [S5].
The bill drew 128 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat, and no Republican [S4].
After the subcommittee referrals, no further action was ever taken: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote [S5].
The bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private detention companies and the county jails that house ICE detainees are better off, because their federal contracts continued unchanged, and the immigration enforcement agencies retained the detention and supervision tools the bill would have removed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private detention contractors kept their ICE contracts

sides.party_line_note: All 128 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, and the Democratic chairmen who held the bill in committee never advanced it — support and inaction both fell along party lines.

industries.industry: Private immigration detention companies (GEO Group, CoreCivic)
industries.note: These companies hold most ICE detainees under per-bed federal contracts; the bill would have banned new contracts and terminated existing ones within three years. Their revenue model depends on keeping detention numbers and bed contracts high, which runs directly against detainees' interest in release and humane conditions.

industries.industry: County and local jails housing ICE detainees
industries.note: The bill phases out the use of any non-DHS facility for immigration detention, ending the rental revenue jails earn from ICE beds. Jails profit from detaining immigrants, so their interest runs against the people in those beds.

The bill bans ankle monitors and other electronic surveillance as conditions of supervision and requires for-profit ATD contracts to be terminated and replaced with nonprofits or government operation. These contractors currently charge for monitoring people who would otherwise be free, so their interest sits against the people they monitor.
